story.title: Thinking in Sign, Dreaming in Motion: Four Deaf Omani Pioneers Reshaping Art, Stage, and Screen

story.meta_description: Meet four deaf Omani pioneers—Marwan Al Zadjali, Amjad Al Maqrashi, Shaima Al Hasani, and Fatima Al Busaidi—transforming theatre, first aid, TV, and fine art.

detail.extracted_title: Thinking in Sign, Dreaming in Motion: Four Deaf Omani Pioneers Reshaping Art, Stage, and Screen
detail.excerpt: Across Oman, four deaf pioneers are demonstrating how the absence of auditory noise sharpens visual attention and creative resolve—from founding a national theatre troupe and earning an international paramedic license to presenting on national television and exhibiting paintings across eight countries.
detail.article_html:
Imagine waking up in a world where the concept of sound does not exist. There is no melody, no street noise, and not even that quiet inner voice that whispers as you read a page. For people born deaf, inner life unfolds through a different architecture altogether: thoughts take shape as vivid visual scenes, memories play out like cinema, and even dreams speak in sign language.

Across the Sultanate of Oman, Marwan Al Zadjali, Amjad Al Maqrashi, Shaima Al Hasani, and Fatima Al Busaidi have turned this heightened visual perception into pioneering achievements in theatre, emergency medicine, broadcast journalism, and fine art.

A Stage Without Spoken Words: Marwan Al Zadjali and the Oman Theatre Troupe for the Deaf

For Marwan bin Ramadhan Al Zadjali, Chairman and co-founder of the Oman Theatre Troupe for the Deaf, the absence of sound is a source of extraordinary mental calm and observational focus. When he reflects on a decision or recalls a memory, his mind operates without spoken words. Abstract concepts such as love, hope, time, and freedom appear as moving cinema inside his imagination. When he sleeps, his dreams unfold with characters and full conversations conducted entirely in sign language.

His passion for theatre began during his primary school years at Al Amal School for the Deaf, where he discovered that facial expressions, posture, and stage movement constituted his truest language. Together with his fellow deaf performers, he later established the Oman Theatre Troupe for the Deaf to give that visual language a permanent home.

The troupe's early years were marked by skepticism. Organizers initially excluded them from theatre festivals inside and outside Oman, doubting that deaf actors could command a stage. Rather than stepping back, the performers treated that doubt as fuel, rehearsing relentlessly until their visual storytelling won over audiences and festival directors alike. Working alongside sign language interpreter Asila Al Maashari, whom members affectionately call the troupe's spiritual mother, the actors built a bridge to hearing audiences while proving that theatre relies on human presence long before spoken dialogue.

Healing Hands and Unbroken Bridges: Amjad Al Maqrashi's First Aid Milestone

When Amjad bint Mohammed Al Maqrashi earned the International First Aid License, she became the first deaf paramedic in Oman and across the Arab world to hold the credential. For her, sign language has been an anchor of identity since her earliest days at Al Amal School for the Deaf, giving her the confidence to step into fields rarely entered by people with hearing impairments.

One encounter remains etched in her memory and continues to guide her community work. Years ago, Amjad and a deaf friend met a young deaf girl who had never been able to complete her schooling. Because the girl had not been taught formal sign language, even Amjad struggled to understand her improvised gestures. That moment left Amjad determined to ensure no deaf person in Oman would be left isolated without a shared language.

Alongside her work in emergency first aid, Amjad is a graphic designer, a lifelong reader of biographies, and an active member of four volunteer teams focused on environmental protection, public health, and financial literacy. She also leads a specialized volunteer team dedicated to supporting and empowering the deaf community across the Sultanate.

Composure Under the Studio Lights: Shaima Al Hasani on Oman Television

Stepping in front of the cameras at Sultanate of Oman Television, Shaima bint Yousef Al Hasani broke new ground as the nation's first television presenter with a hearing impairment. In a broadcast industry built around audio cues and spoken scripts, she relied on patience, visual precision, and quiet self-assurance to claim her place.

In Shaima's inner world, thoughts translate directly into live imagery and signed movements, as though she is conversing with herself through motion. Freed from surrounding chatter, her eyes immediately register the subtle shifts of a guest's posture, a fleeting smile, or the atmosphere of a room.

Entering a workplace dominated by hearing colleagues presented immediate communication hurdles when co-workers did not know sign language. Shaima overcame those barriers by building practical habits around written notes, expressive body language, digital tools, and collaboration with interpreters. What some initially assumed would slow her down in a fast-paced newsroom instead sharpened her eye for detail on screen.

Canvas Across Eight Nations: The Visual Journey of Fatima Al Busaidi

In her early primary school classrooms, Fatima bint Mohammed Al Busaidi often sat watching her teacher speak without understanding a single word. Whenever boredom crept in, she turned her imagination toward her school notebooks and began to draw. Through books and quiet observation, she discovered a visual vocabulary that required no spoken explanation, teaching her classmates to paint and soon winning school art competitions.

Her path as a visual artist was tested early by a painful remark. One day, while she sat painting outdoors, a passerby stopped and asked in disbelief how she could possibly paint when she could neither speak nor hear. Although the comment stung, Fatima made a quiet vow on the spot that she would become a prominent artist whose work spoke for itself.

She kept that promise. Today, Fatima is a pioneering deaf Omani painter and exhibition organizer who leads art workshops for students and represents the Sultanate abroad. Her paintings have traveled to exhibitions in eight countries: Switzerland, Jordan, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, and Egypt. Reflecting on her journey, she notes that whereas her childhood dreams once ran like silent films, today every dream she has speaks fluently in sign language.

detail.instagram_caption:
How does the human mind create when it is completely freed from the noise of the world? For four deaf Omani pioneers, inner thought unfolds as vivid cinema, and even dreams speak in sign language.

Marwan bin Ramadhan Al Zadjali, Chairman and co-founder of the Oman Theatre Troupe for the Deaf, recalls how his troupe was initially excluded from theatre festivals by skeptics who doubted deaf actors could command a stage. Refusing to step back, the performers rehearsed relentlessly alongside sign language interpreter Asila Al Maashari until their visual storytelling reshaped public perception across the Sultanate.

In emergency medicine, Amjad bint Mohammed Al Maqrashi became the first deaf paramedic in Oman and the Arab world to earn the International First Aid License. Alongside her design work, she participates in four volunteer teams and leads a specialized initiative supporting the deaf community.

At Sultanate of Oman Television, Shaima bint Yousef Al Hasani stepped in front of the studio lights as the nation's first television presenter with a hearing impairment, turning heightened visual focus into an asset in a fast-paced newsroom.

And in fine art, painter Fatima bint Mohammed Al Busaidi answered early skepticism with a vow to excel. Starting from sketches in her primary school notebooks, she has exhibited her paintings across eight countries—from Switzerland to Egypt—while organizing exhibitions and student workshops at home.
